name: 分家
highlights: 分家主要有两种方法：长辈年迈或去世后儿子们分家；儿子结婚后即分出单过
分家主持人由家族中有威望的人担当，请娘舅和姑父作证
全家只有一个宅院时，厅堂（西间）留作公用，上大房分长子，下大房分次子
1945年程振兴旅店分家，因东西钱财太多，用去三个多月
程乐涞给七个儿子分家的方式：每个儿子成亲后给本钱和必需品出去单过
content_zh:
分家主要有两种方法，一种是当家里的长辈年迈或去世后，儿子们相互分家，有时也可能是长孙和叔叔们分家。在这种情况下，分家的主持人一般由家族中有威望的人来担当，更重要的是要请娘舅和姑父来作证，找会写字的人来执笔写分家契。

分家的第一步是要把属于大家庭的家产和财务情况做登记。对于一般的人家，分家主要只涉及房产和地产。在分房产的时候，如果全家只有一个宅院，院里的厅堂或称西间，会留作公用，用以举行红白喜事。在西间东侧的叫上大房，会分给长子；西间西侧的叫下大房，会分给次子；余下房间的分法并无特定的模式。对于一些大户人家来讲，分家时家具和器物也都要逐一登记，并力图平均分配。例如，1945年老街上最大的旅店程振兴被一分为二。据说，因为东西和钱财太多，分家前前后后用去了三个多月的时间。

一般来说，长子和有长孙的儿子，在分家时会得到较好的一份。如果当时家里还有未成家的男子，也会得到相应的照顾。这种照顾多局限在钱财或器物上，例如，母亲可能把自己的私房钱分给未婚的儿子。在分家后，如果父母还在世，一般会跟长子一起生活；有些人家，父母也会轮流到几个儿子家居住，享受子女的照顾。

另外一种分家的方法是每当一个儿子结婚以后，父母就会拿出一些钱财和器物，让小两口单过。据程镇康老人讲，其太公程乐涞就是这样给他的七个儿子分家的。当程乐涞帮长子程昭斌成亲后，就给了他两千铜钱、一条扁担、两个布袋、一个锅、几个盆和碗，让他们出去租房单过。别看这几样再普通不过的东西，里面却饱含老人的一片苦心。扁担和布袋是给他到杭州和金华去做茶叶生意；两千铜钱当然就是起家和做生意的本钱；有了锅、盆和碗，就可以起灶做饭，填饱肚子。老人没给被褥之类的东西，是因为这些都来自于随嫁的嫁妆。

对于接下来的五个儿子，老人都是如此：帮他们娶亲，给他们一些本钱和生活的必需品，让他们出去单过。区别只是当家境好的时候，一条扁担可能变成了两条扁担；家境不好的时候，两千铜钱或许变成了五百铜钱；等到最小的儿子程昭祥成家的时候，老人把他留在了身边，帮助料理，并最终继承了家里的小旅店。有趣的是，这六个被扫地出门的儿子，日后都成了颇有成就的大商人，远比备受照顾的小儿子家境好。其中有三个在老街上做起了旅店生意，而且都是赫赫有名的大旅店；另外三个分别经营着茶叶生意、南货店和雨伞店。
content_en:
Family division mainly follows two methods. The first occurs when elders are elderly or deceased, and sons divide the family—sometimes a grandson divides with his uncles. In such cases, the division is presided over by a respected family member, and crucially, maternal uncles and paternal aunts' husbands are invited as witnesses, while a literate person writes the division contract.

The first step is to register all family property and finances. For ordinary families, division mainly involves housing and land. If the family has only one courtyard, the main hall (also called xi jian, west room) is retained for common use, for weddings and funerals. The room east of the west room, called shang da fang (upper great room), goes to the eldest son; the room west of it, xia da fang (lower great room), goes to the second son. The remaining rooms have no fixed division pattern. For wealthy families, furniture and utensils are also registered and distributed as evenly as possible. For example, in 1945 the largest inn on the old street, Cheng Zhenxing, was split in two. Reportedly, because there were so many possessions and money, the division took over three months.

Generally, the eldest son and the son with the eldest grandson receive a better share. Unmarried sons also receive corresponding consideration, usually limited to money or utensils—for example, a mother might give her private savings to an unmarried son. After division, if parents are still alive, they usually live with the eldest son; some families rotate parents among sons' homes.

The second method is that whenever a son marries, the parents give him some money and utensils to set up a separate household. According to Elder Cheng Zhenkang, his great-grandfather Cheng Lelai divided his seven sons this way. When the eldest son Cheng Zhaobin married, Cheng Lelai gave him 2,000 copper coins, one carrying pole, two cloth bags, one pot, and several basins and bowls, letting them rent a place and live independently. These ordinary items carried deep meaning: the pole and bags were for the tea business in Hangzhou and Jinhua; the 2,000 coins were startup capital; the pot, basins, and bowls allowed them to cook and eat. Bedding was not given because it came with the bride's dowry.

The same was done for the next five sons: help them marry, give capital and necessities, and let them live separately. The difference was only in scale—when the family was better off, one pole might become two; when poorer, 2,000 coins might become 500. When the youngest son Cheng Zhaoxiang married, the old man kept him at home to help manage, and he eventually inherited the family's small inn. Interestingly, the six sons sent out all became successful merchants, far better off than the favored youngest. Three opened inns on the old street—all famous large inns; the other three ran a tea business, a dry goods store, and an umbrella shop.
